title: gen-aesop
first: Four fables in the Rev. George Fyler Townsend’s translation
A WOLF who had a bone stuck in his throat hired a Crane, for a large sum, to put her head into his mouth and draw out the bone.

When the Crane had extracted the bone and demanded the promised payment, the Wolf, grinning and grinding his teeth, exclaimed: “Why, you have surely already had a sufficient recompense, in having been permitted to draw out your head in safety from the mouth and jaws of a wolf.”
last: THE SWALLOW and the Crow had a contention about their plumage.
The Crow put an end to the dispute by saying, “Your feathers are all very well in the spring, but mine protect me against the winter.”
Fair weather friends are not worth much.
The same lesson is a Russian proverb: Тише едешь — дальше будешь.
The Greek for a fable is μῦθος, and the fables are online at Project Gutenberg.
